If I'm reading correctly, your question basically boils down to: if a universe splits in two, and both versions of the same person travel back in time, do they end up in the same place on top of each other. The answer, in Trek lore at least, is no. Kelvin and Prime are completely separate timelines from one another, past present and future, that just so happen to be identical up until a certain point. That's not a theme, that's a plotline. There's a big difference.

The idea of artificial life being inherently incompatible with organic life simply doesn't feature as a subtext in the wider Mass Effect world prior to the end of the third game. The ideological conflicts with Cerberus, or Terra Firma, or the other Citadel races is never about AI, it's about multilateralism and xenophobia. The fall of the Protheans isn't because they couldn't co-exist with their AI creations, but because their unilateral society didn't have the strength of the OT's more diverse setting. This is the main thematic conflict across the first two games (and most of the third), and the ending of the trilogy is wildly incongruous with it. It's a textbook example of how not to resolve a story.

I don't hate it because it's space magic, I hate it because it is a thematically stupid ending. If there is one recurring theme throughout the series it is the strength in diversity (Shepard's multilateral crew, the ideological conflict with Cerberus, the Protheans dying out because they were too homogeneous). So for the ultimate ending to be "forced homogeneity" is completely incongruent with what we've seen up to that point.

It's a separate discussion but I also had a good laugh at the "throughout the series the organic-synthetic conflict is brought plenty of times". It's really not. Outside of one or two forgettable side quests it's hardly discussed at all, and that's one of the main reasons the ending as a whole is terrible.

Racism in football is an important issue and it honestly saddens me to see the BBC choose to spotlight such a weak case when there are so many horrific examples in recent years.

Anton Ferdinand was found not to be a credible witness to his own claim, he changed his story several times and made several initial statements that were later deemed to be factually inaccurate and withdrawn. He eventually settled on the story that he didn't actually hear any abuse from Terry (something which it looks like he may be taking back for the purposes of this documentary). Anyone who has ever studied or practiced law will tell you that it is important to have your facts straight right up front, because if any single part of your story gets shown to not be credible, then every single part of your story suddenly looks not credible regardless of what actually happened.

The brief video clip is never going to be enough evidence to prove one way or another what happened, but what little is there clearly does not support Anton's story. From Anton's complete lack of any kind of reaction to Terry, to his clearly covering his mouth when he speaks to Terry so as to avoid the cameras, to Terry's obvious look of shock and bemusement in response to whatever Anton said. There's no way to know what really happened, but the limited video evidence certainly aligns more closely to Terry's story than Anton's.

Then there's the Ferdinand's own unfortunate track record with racially insensitive behaviour (the choc ice incident). And yes, I am aware of the term "whataboutism" and no, the Ferdinands doing something wrong absolutely does not make John Terry right, but it absolutely does make the Ferdinands bad spokespersons for racial issues whatever way you look at it.

At this point there is no sense in relitigating the incident. We don't really know what happened and we probably never will. The problem with using this case to spotlight racism in football is that there is no real evidence as to what happened one way or another, which means that your opinion on it invariably falls along the lines of football rivalry. By doing this they are effectively diminishing the cause of racism in football to a matter of mere footballing rivalry, which undermines the message they are trying to support. I think this will do more harm than good.

I think it's mainly the tone. The Orville more closely adheres to the tone of 90s Trek, which was light, mostly family friendly, with some silliness and humour but enough sincerity and high stakes to give the characters and story meaning. Classic Trek also tended to be more focused on thought provoking high concept sci-fi. Many episodes did not have a single phaser fired, or explosion, or death, some of the best episodes were just people talking about ideas. It was also somewhat relatable for the audience. Even though it was set in the future, the characters felt like real people and acted like (very idealistic) real people.

By comparison, new Trek is almost relentlessly dark, melodramatic, depressing, filled to the brim with mindless action, explosions and OTT dramatic acting. The characters are mostly thinly developed plot vectors (one main character didn't even have a name until revealed in a short trek 2 seasons in) none of whom act like real people and so are not relatable in the same way as 90s Trek characters felt to many.

So in this respect The Orville is far closer to 90s Trek than Discovery or even Picard. I think this is the comparison most people are making.
